nodes.partnerMessage:
Flight cases are finally inside. Deadbolt's locked, stage sign is off, and I can actually hear myself think.

You really came into the private room, {PlayerName}.

I'm on this horrible swivel stool in an oversized flannel, half my makeup is gone, and my ears are still humming from the set.

I know the version of me people usually see is loud and restless and always doing something. Right now I'm honestly just tired.

So tell me straight. Did you come for the DJ version of me, or did you actually want to meet the person underneath all that noise?

choices.choiceText: I'm here for the sound nerd behind the mixer. The stage lights don't matter to me.
I came to check on you. Carrying heavy gear home at 4:30 AM takes a real toll.
I wanted to hear that private, uncompressed acoustic draft you talked about.
Just seeing if you're as wild and hyperactive in private as you are in the club.
Can I meet the version of you that never gets on a stage?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. That actually gets to me a little.

At the club, everybody wants more of the same version of me. Louder. Faster. Stay up longer. Keep the room moving.

I like that version too, but I can't be her every second I'm awake.

Sometimes I get home after a great night and realize I haven't had one quiet conversation all evening.

So having you here, not asking me to perform, feels really good.

choices.choiceText: The knob is at zero tonight, Trixie. You don't have to entertain me.
Does the party girl persona get exhausting to carry around all the time?
How are your ears holding up after that four-hour set?
What are you like when the crowd finally goes home?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Pretty wrecked, actually. My shoulders are killing me and my hands still smell like metal from the case handles.

The glamorous part is two hours on a stage. The rest is loading gear into a van, carrying it through an alley, waiting around while someone can't find the right cable, then getting home when normal people are already asleep.

It's weirdly nice that you noticed the boring part.

choices.choiceText: Next time, you text me when your set wraps up. I'm helping you carry that case.
Sit back from the desk. Drop your shoulders away from your ears for a minute.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah, I still have it open.

It's not finished, so don't expect some perfect mastered thing. You can hear the room, the little timing slips, even my chair moving when I leaned forward.

I almost deleted it because it felt too personal.

Give me a second. I'll pull up the section I was talking about.

choices.choiceText: Examine the unreleased stem track diagram.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...Okay.

I know you were trying to joke, but I don't really want to be somebody's idea of a "wild DJ girl" when I'm in my own room.

I'm energetic at work because I love what I do. That's different from wanting to be treated like a spectacle when the night is over.

I'm still just a person in here. I'd rather you ask me what I'm like than decide for me.

choices.choiceText: I phrased that carelessly, Trixie. I was trying to joke and it fell flat. I'm sorry.
Don't put it in your bio if you don't want people talking about it.

nodes.partnerMessage:
*long breath*

Yeah. Nothing playing.

It's weird how loud silence feels after four hours of speakers and people yelling near the booth. Give me five minutes and my whole body starts unclenching.

I think I forgot how nice it is to be around someone who doesn't need me to keep the energy going.

choices.choiceText: You don't need strobes or subwoofers for me to think you're incredible, Trixie.
What do your ears hear when the studio goes this quiet?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. More than I let people see.

If I'm quiet at a show, someone asks if I'm sick. If I leave an afterparty early, people act like something's wrong.

Eventually you start making the joke before anyone else can. "Oh, there goes Trixie being insane again."

It's easier than explaining that sometimes I just want to go home, take a shower, and eat something in peace.

choices.choiceText: I'll make you breakfast anytime, Trixie. Scrambled eggs, hot coffee, and total silence.
How long have you felt like you had to perform that character?

nodes.partnerMessage:
There's still a little ringing. It usually fades, but the first quiet hour after a set can be the worst part.

I use proper ear protection, keep my booth levels under control, all of that. I know the rules.

That doesn't stop me from worrying about it, though.

My ears are how I work, but they're also how I enjoy music. That's a pretty scary thing to imagine losing.

choices.choiceText: That fear makes complete sense. You're an acoustic artist protecting her instruments.
Focus on the sound of my voice instead of the whistle. Let me be your frequency tonight.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...You know what's funny? People offer me drinks all the time. They offer backstage passes, rides, introductions, all kinds of things.

Nobody says, "Give me the heavy case."

That's such a small thing, but it tells me you're paying attention to what my night actually looks like.

I'm not very good at letting people help me. I probably should learn.

choices.choiceText: You don't need your guard up here. Rest your arms on your desk.
I mean every word. Next gig, you're not lifting that flight case alone.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay. Shoulders down. Feet on the crate.

Oh wow. I really was sitting like I was still behind the decks.

The room smells like spearmint gum and warm electronics. There are cables everywhere and three things on my desk that I probably should have put away hours ago.

This is what I actually look like after a show.

choices.choiceText: Patch cables hanging like vines in an electric jungle. Show me what you've been working on.
Stay right there on that chair. What were you thinking about on the drive home?

nodes.partnerMessage:
See that dip right there? That's the kick making room for the sub.

I spent way too long getting that balance right because I wanted the bass to feel heavy without swallowing the guitar.

Three nights, one thirty-second section. That's the kind of thing that makes me sound completely unreasonable when I explain my job to normal people.

choices.choiceText: That sidechain curve is surgical. You can see the space you carved for the acoustic body.
Where did you record that acoustic guitar sample in the first place?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Thanks. I appreciate the apology.

I can take a joke. I just get tired of the same joke over and over because people think that's the easiest version of me to understand.

So... we're good. Start again. Tell me what kind of music you actually listen to when nobody else is around.

choices.choiceText: Warm, honest sounds. Music that feels like someone built it with their bare hands.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...Great. Now I'm blushing in my own studio.

I think I make everything loud because being loud is easy. Everyone understands it. Nobody has to wonder what you're feeling if you're jumping around and making the room shake.

The quiet version of me is harder to explain.

She's the one who actually wants somebody to know her.

choices.choiceText: I notice how quiet you are. And it's my favorite part of you.
What's patched into your modular synth rack tonight?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, that's actually my ideal morning.

Eggs, real coffee, sunlight, no speakers, no venue schedule.

I don't need much after a week of noise. Give me a kitchen and somebody I genuinely like being around and I'm good.

Honestly, that sounds better than half the parties I get invited to.

choices.choiceText: Don't you dare forfeit your residency. I'll make the eggs after your Friday set.

nodes.partnerMessage:
A few years.

At first I didn't care. The energetic persona got me booked, and I needed the work. Then it became the only thing people wanted from me.

I could send a slower track and they'd tell me to make it bigger. I'd play something weird and they'd ask where the drop was.

So I started saving the stuff I actually cared about for home.

choices.choiceText: Their loss. Your bedroom is where the real art has always lived.
Tonight you don't have to play bangers for anyone. Show me what you really love.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. My dad used to worry about it too.

He repaired instruments, so he was always talking about hearing as if it were something you had to protect for your whole life. I used to roll my eyes when I was younger.

Now every time the ringing gets bad after a show, I hear him in the back of my head telling me not to be stupid.

Annoyingly, he was usually right.

choices.choiceText: He taught you well. Your ears are safe tonight. Rest them in the dark.
Do you still have any of his instrument repair tools?

nodes.partnerMessage:
...That actually helps.

The ringing is still there, but I'm thinking about it less.

It's kind of strange that your voice can cut through all that noise without you even trying.

I was supposed to show you a synth patch tonight and somehow we ended up talking about the parts of me nobody usually gets to see.

choices.choiceText: I'm right here in your monitors, Trixie. No distortion, no clipping.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I was thinking about how weird the drop after a gig is.

You can have three hundred people shouting your name and twenty minutes later you're alone in a car watching the wipers move across wet glass.

The contrast is brutal sometimes. You go from too much attention to none at all.

Your message waiting for me when I got home made that part a little easier.

choices.choiceText: I'll always be there to catch you on that drive home, Trixie.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Wait, you actually noticed that?

Okay. I like you a little more now.

Most people hear the finished track and never think about how much work went into making two sounds stop fighting each other.

That little gap is the trick. Leave room for the guitar and the bass suddenly feels bigger without just making it louder.

choices.choiceText: Only for you, Trixie. Where did the acoustic guitar sample come from?

nodes.partnerMessage:
The guitar belonged to my dad.

It's old and kind of beat up. One tuning peg sticks, there's a scratch across the back, and the case smells like his workshop.

I recorded it late one night because I was too embarrassed to let anyone hear what I was doing. Then I put it next to this huge modern bassline and somehow it worked.

It felt like two parts of my life finally talking to each other.

choices.choiceText: Club promoters don't know soul from static. That sample is your heart on tape.
Your dad's guitar living inside your modern tracks... that's a beautiful legacy.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Stop.

I'm trying very hard to keep the cool DJ thing going here.

You say one nice thing and suddenly I'm hiding my face behind an empty matcha can.

Come on. I'll show you the synth rack before I get any more embarrassed.

choices.choiceText: Show me the hardware, Trixie.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Deal. Sunday morning after the Friday set.

I'll make the eggs. You handle coffee. Nobody is allowed to talk about work for the first hour.

...Okay, maybe that's impossible. But we can try.

Now look at this patch before I lose the idea.

choices.choiceText: Show me the patch.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Exactly. In here, nobody's checking ticket numbers.

I can let a sound sit there for ten minutes because I like the way the room changes around it.

That's probably the part I love most.

The stage version of me has to keep moving. The person in this room gets to stay still.

choices.choiceText: That's pure sound design. Show me that drone.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. I still have them.

They're on a shelf above the interface. I barely use them anymore, but I never moved them.

He had this habit of telling me to slow down whenever I got frustrated. I hated hearing it when I was sixteen.

Now I catch myself saying the same thing to my own equipment.

choices.choiceText: He would be so proud of the engineer and artist you grew into, Trixie.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Don't make promises you don't mean, okay?

I've had people promise they'd be there before. Usually they meant while the night was fun.

It's the quiet part that tells you who actually stays.

So when you say that... I want to believe you. That's the part that scares me.

choices.choiceText: Hold onto me as tight as you need. I'm not letting go.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. That's the bit I really care about.

Dad's guitar, a little tape hiss, a slow delay, and then this stupidly deep bass underneath it.

It's not what people expect from me. Maybe that's why I like it.

Nobody can tell me I'm doing the job wrong when I'm making something that only has to make sense to me.

choices.choiceText: Examine the Eurorack patch routing map.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Thank you.

He always said instruments need people to keep them alive. I think I carried that idea over into everything I make.

That guitar is one of the few things I still have that sounds exactly like him.

So yeah... I like having him somewhere inside the music.

choices.choiceText: He is in the mix. And the sound is stunning. Show me the patch map.
Tell me one thing you still remember about your dad.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, gear time.

Three rows of modules, way too many patch cables, and a power supply I keep promising myself I'll tidy up.

This oscillator feeds the filter, the clock is controlling the delay, and I leave some of the routing slightly unpredictable on purpose.

I like when the machine gives me something I didn't ask for.

choices.choiceText: That clock divider routing creates a natural, breathing pulse. It's brilliant.
Is your power supply properly isolated? All those modules draw heavy amperage.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Every cable has a job. I use the colors so I don't lose track when I'm tired.

I was getting ready to bounce the track when I heard that buzzing again from the power strip.

I've been meaning to fix it. I just kept putting it off because I wanted to finish the music first.

choices.choiceText: A buzzing power strip?! Check the ground loop right now, Trixie!

nodes.partnerMessage:
That's what I was after. I wanted it to move a little like breathing instead of snapping perfectly to a grid.

Wait.

...Did that just spark?

Hold on. I need to look at the rack.

choices.choiceText: Trixie?! Did a capacitor just short out?!

nodes.partnerMessage:
The interface ground is humming through the rack.

That's definitely not normal.

Wait—

*sharp electrical squeal through the monitors*

Oh my God. Nope. That's feedback. I need to kill the power right now.

choices.choiceText: Trixie! Pull the master power switch! Talk to me!

nodes.partnerMessage:
The monitors just screamed.

There was this horrible high sound and now my ears are ringing so hard I can't think. The rack is still buzzing and I don't want to touch another cable while I'm shaking like this.

I'm on the floor. I'm breathing too fast.

Please stay with me.

Hit the call button. I need your voice right now.

choices.choiceText: Connecting to Trixie's studio line (Call 1 - Feedback Emergency)...

nodes.partnerMessage:
*ragged breathing, the last faint electronic hiss in the room*

Please answer.

Just talk to me.

*long, shaky breath*

Main breaker is off. Everything's unplugged.

The ringing is still there, but the room itself is quiet now. I'm sitting under the desk because I don't really trust myself to stand up yet.

I know I probably sounded completely out of control. I was.

You kept talking until I could breathe again. Thank you.

choices.choiceText: You're safe now, Trixie. The power is cut. Just keep your head resting on your knees.
How is the ringing in your ears right now? Did the spike settle down?
Sitting under a studio desk in the dark... you sound so gentle when the volume is gone.
Did any of your analog hardware get damaged in the surge?
Now that you are calm, what do you actually want right now?

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah. I'm staying here for a minute.

The floor is cool and the desk is blocking out all the blinking lights.

If you hadn't been talking to me, I probably would have panicked and started yanking cables out at random.

That would have been a terrible idea. Thanks for keeping me from making it worse.

choices.choiceText: I'll always be your anchor when the frequencies get chaotic, Trixie.
Take all the time you need under that desk. I'm right here on the line.

nodes.partnerMessage:
The spike has settled. There's still a thin ringing in the background, but it's not getting louder.

I'm using my soft earplugs and keeping everything quiet for now.

I'm not going to pretend I wasn't scared, though. That sound was bad.

choices.choiceText: Smart girl. Keep those earplugs in and let your eardrums recover.

nodes.partnerMessage:
This is the part nobody sees.

On stage I'm loud because I know exactly what people expect from me. Confidence. Energy. Never looking overwhelmed.

Down here I'm just twenty-two and exhausted, and honestly a little afraid of what it feels like when the crowd disappears.

I don't always know how to switch from "performing" back to being a normal person.

choices.choiceText: You don't have to be ten feet tall for me, Trixie. The girl on the carpet is the one I care about.
You'll never be alone in the quiet again. I'm in your corner.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Looks like I blew a fuse. That's it. The important gear is okay.

Honestly, I'm more upset about what happened to my head than the hardware.

Machines can be repaired. I was scared of being alone in that room when everything went wrong. You staying mattered a lot more than the equipment did.

choices.choiceText: Because you're worth showing up for, Trixie. Every single time.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...Okay.

People usually tell me to turn the volume up when I'm overwhelmed.

You're the first person who's made quiet feel safe.

I didn't know how much I needed that until tonight.

choices.choiceText: Silence is where you find yourself again. Come out from under the desk when you're ready.

nodes.partnerMessage:
...Yeah. The girl on the carpet.

That's me without the lights, makeup, noise, or stupid confidence routine.

I don't know why showing this version feels harder than standing in front of a packed warehouse.

Maybe because the stage version can always hide behind the music. This one is just me.

choices.choiceText: You are grounded now, Trixie. Step out from under the desk.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay. I'm out.

The monitors are dark. The computer is quiet. Nothing is blinking at me anymore.

And the sky is getting lighter.

That's actually the first time all night I've looked out the window instead of at a screen.

choices.choiceText: Dawn light on the fire escapes... that sounds like a peaceful view.
How does the room feel now that all the machines are sleeping?
You don't have to fill the quiet. You can just be here with me.

nodes.partnerMessage:
It's that weird blue-purple color right before sunrise properly starts.

There's a street cleaner somewhere down the block and birds are starting up on the roof.

Everything looks softer at this hour.

Like the city hasn't decided what it wants from me yet.

choices.choiceText: Let's hold our breath with it. Just you and me in the blue light.

nodes.partnerMessage:
It feels like my room again.

When everything is running, it feels like work. When it's all off, it's just my messy bedroom with cables everywhere.

I actually like it better like this.

Less impressive. More mine.

choices.choiceText: Good. Because your room is for you and me tonight. Not the crowd.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I found the old cassette recorder.

It's battery powered, so it doesn't need the wall at all.

I still have that little recording of Dad's guitar on it. It's not polished. You can hear the tape hiss and the room around it.

I want you to hear it. Not because it's some huge artistic statement. I just want to share something that actually means something to me.

Call me one more time, {PlayerName}. Let the tape run while morning comes in.

choices.choiceText: Connecting to Trixie's dawn line (Call 2 - Tape Hiss and Sunrise)...

nodes.partnerMessage:
*soft tape hiss, a small mechanical click, then quiet guitar notes through the receiver*

...You're there.

Okay. Don't say anything yet.

Just listen with me for a minute.

*quiet voice note from bed*

Tape's off. Curtains are open. It's morning.

My ears feel better, and now that I'm not running on adrenaline, I'm realizing how tired I am.

That recording sounded different with you listening. Maybe because I wasn't thinking about whether anybody else would like it. I just wanted you to hear it.

Sunday morning at nine. I'll make breakfast. Come sit with me and let me be a normal person for a while.

choices.choiceText: Sunday morning at nine. I'll be there with hot coffee, Trixie. Sleep peacefully.
I'll be knocking on your door at 8:59 AM sharp. It's a date.
Before breakfast, tell me what you want the morning to feel like.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Sunday at nine.

No club. No flight cases. No one asking for another track. Just breakfast, coffee, and a morning where we can talk without shouting.

That sounds ridiculously good to me right now.

Goodnight, {PlayerName}. Thanks for staying when things got ugly. Sleep well.

Status: Read just now.

Trixie has switched studio mode to "Do Not Disturb."

choices.choiceText: Trixie? Did the studio interface crash?
I'm sorry, Trixie. I made a lazy joke about you being wild and it was disrespectful. Please let me start over.
Leaving people on read after performing all night is pretty dramatic.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Status: Read 30m ago.

[Typing...]

Trixie has muted notifications for this session.

The call dropped while everything was still settling down.

I'm still in the studio with the master power off.

My ears are okay enough for the moment, but I really don't want to sit here alone for too long.

Call me back when your connection is stable.

choices.choiceText: Signal reconnected! Calling back right now!

nodes.partnerMessage:
I think I'm going to leave it here.

We want different things, and I don't have the energy to keep forcing a conversation that isn't working.

No hard feelings. Take care of yourself.

I spend enough time dealing with people who think they can treat me however they want because I'm the person working the room.

I'm not bringing that into my own space.

I'm ending the conversation here. Take care.

Okay, then let me answer a question I don't get asked very often.

When I'm not DJing, I'm actually pretty boring.

I sleep late. I make too much coffee. I leave three different projects open on my laptop and forget which one I was supposed to finish. I go to the grocery store in a hoodie and hope nobody recognizes me.

Sometimes I don't listen to music at all.

Sometimes I just want to sit somewhere with somebody and talk about absolutely nothing.

That probably sounds less exciting than "wild underground DJ," but it's the version of me I trust more.

choices.choiceText: That sounds exactly like the version of you I want to know.
What is something you do when nobody is around that you would never post online?

nodes.partnerMessage:
You know what?

I've been talking about myself for basically the entire night.

Tell me something about you that isn't on your profile.

Not your job. Not your music taste. Not some impressive answer.

Something ordinary.

I want to know what you're like when nobody is watching too.

choices.choiceText: I like quiet mornings, good food, and being around someone who doesn't make me pretend.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah.

I think that's why this feels easy.

We're both talking about the same thing without really saying it.

Not having to perform. Not having to be interesting every second.

Just having someone there and being okay with the quiet.

That's probably what I want more than another exciting night.

choices.choiceText: Then let tonight be quiet. You don't have to keep me entertained.

nodes.partnerMessage:
After a good gig?

I get home, kick my shoes off, take a shower that's way too hot, and stand in the kitchen trying to decide whether I'm actually hungry or just tired.

Usually I make eggs.

Sometimes I eat them standing at the counter because sitting down feels like too much effort.

Then I put my phone on Do Not Disturb and stare at the ceiling for twenty minutes.

Very glamorous lifestyle.

choices.choiceText: That sounds kind of peaceful, actually.

nodes.partnerMessage:
It is.

That's probably why I keep wanting someone to be there for it.

Not to make the moment bigger.

Just to sit across from me while I eat something terrible at one in the morning and complain about how cold the apartment is.

I think that's my version of romance.

Very glamorous. Very mature.

choices.choiceText: I would happily sit across from you while you complain about your cold apartment.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Okay, wow.

You're making this dangerously easy.

I was prepared for flirting to feel like a joke. Something light that disappears when the night is over.

Now I'm sitting here thinking about what it would actually be like to have you in my kitchen after a gig.

You eating eggs. Me complaining. Both of us too tired to pretend we're cooler than we are.

That sounds... really good.

choices.choiceText: Then let's make the boring version of us happen too.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I like that.

A date without music.

No headphones. No playlist debate. No "listen to this drop." No trying to impress each other with obscure artists.

Just food, a table, and whatever we end up talking about.

Maybe I'll discover you have terrible opinions about breakfast.

That would be a dealbreaker, obviously.

choices.choiceText: You can judge my breakfast opinions over coffee on Sunday.

nodes.partnerMessage:
I talk to myself when I'm working.

Not in a concerning way. I just mutter things like, "Why did I do that?" or "Come on, just behave," to a synth that obviously cannot hear me.

I also name unfinished tracks terrible temporary names so I don't get attached to them.

There's one called "DO NOT OPEN THIS FILE" that I've been working on for six months.

I refuse to rename it now.

choices.choiceText: I absolutely want to hear the track you named DO NOT OPEN THIS FILE.

nodes.partnerMessage:
One thing I remember about him?

He always had coffee on the workbench, even when he swore he was cutting back.

He'd be repairing something with those little tools spread everywhere, music playing quietly in the background, and he'd hum along without realizing it.

I used to think it was annoying.

Now I catch myself doing the exact same thing.

That's probably how you realize someone really stayed with you.

choices.choiceText: You kept more of him than you probably realized.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Right now?

Honestly, I want food and sleep.

And maybe another ten minutes talking to you before I crash.

I know that isn't a very romantic answer.

But after tonight, normal sounds pretty romantic to me.

I don't need some giant moment.

I'm happy just knowing the person I wanted to talk to is still here.

choices.choiceText: Then take your ten minutes. I'm still here.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Sunday at nine it is.

I'll probably be half asleep, hair everywhere, wearing the oldest hoodie I own.

The kitchen will be a mess because I never clean before coffee.

You can have the good mug. I have one that says "probably not a morning person," and it's painfully accurate.

We'll eat, talk, and see where the morning goes.

No pressure to make it into some huge romantic thing.

Just come over.

choices.choiceText: That sounds better than any perfect date you could have planned.

nodes.partnerMessage:
Yeah.

I think I needed to hear that.

I've spent a lot of time making myself into someone people can get excited about.

I don't think I've spent enough time being someone people can simply stay with.

Maybe Sunday can be the start of that.

For now, I should probably stop pretending I'm not exhausted and actually sleep.

choices.choiceText: Get some sleep. I'll see you Sunday morning.
